issues.legal_issue: The retroactive application of a restriction on eviction suits brought by a transferee landlord does not unreasonably infringe the constitutional right to property.
material_facts: The landlord acquired the property by transfer and brought an eviction suit within three years of acquiring it.
A later amendment made the restriction on such suits apply retroactively to pending suits and appeals.
The tenant argued that this retroactive application was unconstitutional.
issues.conclusion: The retroactive operation of the restriction was not unreasonable and did not offend Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed B. Banerjee v. Anita Pan, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 774, which upheld the validity of the retroactive application of the amendment under Article 19(1)(f), read with Article 19(5).

predicates.tenancy_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding to recover possession from a tenant.
predicates.transferee_landlord_filed_suit_within_re: A landlord who acquired an interest by transfer brought the eviction suit before the newly imposed waiting period had elapsed.
predicates.later_law_applied_restriction_to_pending: A later legal change applied the restriction to proceedings that were already pending.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding involves a transferee landlord who sued within a later-imposed restricted period and a subsequent legal change applies that restriction to pending cases, the retroactive operation does not unreasonably infringe property rights.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may permit amendment of pleadings to address a change in law affecting a pending proceeding, while giving the opposing party an opportunity to respond.
material_facts: While the Letters Patent appeal was pending, the law applicable to the eviction suit had changed retroactively.
The landlord sought and obtained leave to amend the plaint to address the change.
The tenant filed an additional written statement in response to the amended plaint.
issues.conclusion: The court hearing the Letters Patent appeal could permit amendment of the pleadings and give the opposing party an opportunity to answer the amended case.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the approach in B. Banerjee v. Anita Pan, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 774, for working out the mechanics of applying the retroactive amendment to pending litigation. It also referred to Order 6, Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, under which amendment may be permitted at a stage that can include an appeal or second appeal.

predicates.pending_appeal_affected_by_change_in_law: An appeal was pending when a change in law affected the case.
predicates.pleadings_need_adjustment_to_address_tha: A party's existing pleadings did not address matters made relevant by the change in law.

issues.definition: When a pending appeal is affected by a change in law and the pleadings need adjustment to address it, the appellate court may permit amendment while allowing the opposing party to respond.

issues.legal_issue: A Letters Patent appellate bench hearing an appeal from a second appeal cannot itself resolve new disputed factual issues that require additional evidence and fresh fact-finding.
material_facts: The Letters Patent appeal arose from a judgment disposing of a second appeal.
After the pleadings were amended, new disputed issues arose about the landlord's need for the premises and the availability of suitable accommodation.
The appellate bench permitted oral and documentary evidence, assessed it, and made factual findings on those issues.
The amended issues required fresh fact-finding that had not been undertaken by the trial court or the first appellate court.
issues.conclusion: The appellate bench could not take and assess the new evidence and make findings on the fresh disputed factual issues; the matter had to be remanded for fact-finding by the appropriate lower court.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 100 and 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure limit a High Court's role in a second appeal: its power to determine facts is confined to specified circumstances and to evidence on the record. An appeal under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent from a decision in second appeal is subject to those same limits. Order 41, Rule 27 concerns admission of additional evidence and does not authorize the appellate court to undertake fresh trial-level assessment of disputed facts. The Court distinguished admitting evidence from appreciating it and acting on it, and held Indrajit Pratap Sahi v. Amar Singh, 50 I.A. 183, and Surinder Kumar v. Gian Chand, [1958] S.C.R. 548, inapplicable to that question.

predicates.letters_patent_appeal_from_second_appeal: A Letters Patent appeal was brought from a judgment disposing of a second appeal.
predicates.amended_pleadings_created_new_disputed_f: Amended pleadings introduced factual disputes that had not previously been part of the case.
predicates.additional_evidence_needed_for_fresh_fac: Resolving the new factual disputes required additional evidence and its assessment.

issues.definition: When a Letters Patent appeal from a second appeal involves new factual disputes raised by amended pleadings that require additional evidence and fresh fact-finding, those factual issues must be remitted to a lower court.

issues.legal_issue: A party's consent or failure to object cannot confer on a court inherent jurisdiction that it does not possess.
material_facts: In the Letters Patent appeal from the second appeal, the appellate bench took oral evidence on factual issues newly raised by amended pleadings.
The tenant had not objected to the appellate bench taking that evidence.
The new issues required fact-finding beyond the appellate bench's authorized role.
issues.conclusion: The tenant's failure to object did not give the appellate bench jurisdiction to receive and assess the new evidence and make findings of fact.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the rule that consent cannot confer inherent jurisdiction, relying on Ledgard v. Bull, 13 I.A. 134 at 145, and Meenakshi Naidoo v. Subramaniya Sastri, 14 I.A. 160.

predicates.letters_patent_appeal_from_second_appeal: A Letters Patent appeal was brought from a judgment disposing of a second appeal.
predicates.new_disputed_facts_required_trial_level_: New factual disputes required evidence to be assessed and findings to be made at the trial or first-appellate level.
predicates.appellant_failed_to_object_to_evidence: The appellant did not object when the appellate court received evidence on the new factual disputes.

issues.definition: When a Letters Patent appeal from a second appeal involves new factual disputes requiring lower-court assessment, the appellant's failure to object to evidence-taking does not confer the missing jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A contention that is implicit in the grounds on which special leave was limited may be considered when those grounds are construed broadly rather than literally.
material_facts: Special leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was limited to specified grounds concerning the effect of the amended eviction law and the enforceability of the decree.
The tenant's jurisdictional contention concerned whether amendment of the pleadings could make competent a suit that was incompetent when instituted.
The Court found that this contention was implicit in the permitted grounds when those grounds were read as a connected grievance.
issues.conclusion: The Court could entertain the jurisdictional contention because it was implicit in the grounds covered by the limited grant of special leave.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 permits special leave to be limited to specified points, in which case the appeal cannot extend to unrelated matters; however, the permitted grounds must be construed broadly to identify the real contention, not narrowly or grammatically. The Court relied on Nafe Singh v. State of Haryana, [1971] 3 S.C.C. 934, and Jagdev Singh v. State of Punjab, A.I.R. 1973 S.C. 2427, on the limits of a restricted grant, and distinguished Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma, [1964] 2 S.C.R. 933, which concerned an appeal on a certificate. It also noted that, in exceptional cases and subject to fair notice and opportunity, Article 137 permits review of an order limiting leave so as to expand the leave in the interests of justice.

predicates.supreme_court_special_leave_appeal: The proceeding before the Supreme Court was an appeal brought after special leave had been granted.
predicates.leave_limited_to_related_grounds: The grant of special leave confined the appeal to specified grounds.
predicates.contention_is_implicit_in_permitted_grou: The disputed contention formed part of the real grievance expressed in the permitted grounds, even if it was not stated there expressly.

issues.definition: In an appeal under limited special leave, a contention implicit in the permitted grounds falls within the appeal when those grounds are read to identify their real and related grievance.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory remedy for setting aside certain eviction decrees is additional to, and does not displace, a tenant's pending appeal challenging the competence of the suit.
material_facts: The tenant had a pending appeal challenging an eviction decree obtained by a transferee landlord.
The tenant had also applied for relief under the separate statutory remedy, but that application was rejected for want of prosecution.
The landlord argued that the tenant's failure to obtain relief through that remedy prevented the tenant from challenging the decree in the pending appeal.
issues.conclusion: The separate remedy was additional rather than exclusive; the tenant could still challenge the suit's competence in the pending appeal, and the unsuccessful application did not bar that appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17E of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, provided a remedy to set aside specified eviction decrees, particularly where no appeal was pending and the tenant had not yet been physically evicted. The Court held that the remedy supplemented rather than displaced a pending appeal raising the effect of Section 13(3A), and that Section 17E did not make such an appeal incompetent.

predicates.eviction_decree_based_on_covered_ground: An eviction decree was based on a ground for which a separate statutory setting-aside remedy was provided.
predicates.tenant_appeal_pending: The tenant had an appeal against the eviction decree pending.
predicates.separate_decree_relief_not_obtained: The tenant did not obtain relief through the separate procedure for setting aside the decree.

issues.definition: When an eviction decree based on a covered ground is under appeal and the tenant has not obtained relief through a separate setting-aside procedure, the pending appeal remains available to challenge the suit.
